title: Guru Angad close
hookLine: the second Guru taught the script, the body and a few sharp lines

lines: A WRESTLING GROUND, A PAGE OF LETTERS.
cards: A patch of packed earth where young men wrestle in the early morning, dust on their shoulders. A page of letters copied out in a careful, rounded hand.
A long row of people sitting on the floor, being handed bowls of rice pudding. And a handful of short verses, tucked into the ballads of the Granth. Four pictures, one life.
Tradition connects each of them to Guru Angad, the quiet successor: the script, the body, the kitchen, and the few sharp lines.

teach.b: Start with the letters. Tradition says Guru Angad gave shape to the Gurmukhi script and taught it, so ordinary people could read and write the Gurus' words in their own language. Then the body.

Tradition says he set up wrestling grounds at Khadur and encouraged exercise and strength. A healthy body, in this telling, isn't a distraction from the spiritual life; it's part of a life that can serve.

Then the kitchen, and here the Granth itself speaks. In a ballad by the bards Satta and Balvand, his wife, Mata Khivi, is praised, in paraphrase, as a good woman who gives shade like a tree full of leaves.
In the langar, it says, wealth is shared out, and rice pudding with ghee is served, sweet as nectar. And then the lines themselves, from these four days. See without eyes, walk without feet.
A hundred moons and a thousand suns, and still darkness without the Guru. Service spoiled by pride. Ego as a long illness, with its medicine inside.
Put it together and a style shows. Nothing wasted. A script so people could read.
A body kept ready. A kitchen that feeds.

teach.h: THE LINES: SHORT, AND STILL CUTTING.
teach.b: And verses short enough for the palm of your hand, sharp enough to still cut through. That's what the second Guru left: not volume, but edge.
That's today's line: short and sharp.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Angad in the ardas and on his gurpurab, read his saloks within the Vars, and tell of Mata Khivi's langar when they speak of the free kitchen's history.

games.q: you're the second Guru, and ordinary people can't read the Gurus' words in their own language. what does tradition say you do?
o: give shape to the Gurmukhi script and teach it.
games.why: tradition says Guru Angad gave shape to Gurmukhi and taught it, so the Word could be read by ordinary people.

practice: Let this week's pictures pass by, the muddy grass, the hundred moons, the illness with its cure, and ask what one thing you've learned lately, about your work, your people or yourself.
Say it in a single short sentence, cut a word, then another, and when it's as short as it can be, hold it on the breath. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Guru Angad close. The second Guru: tradition credits him with the script and the wrestling ground, the Granth praises Mata Khivi's langar, and his saloks are few lines that cut deep. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: short and sharp. Tomorrow, the old Guru's voice. That's today, done.
